description:
Could You Ride NASA's Biggest Planetary Spacecraft?

Episode 95 of a daily journey through the universe. 🚀
We ride with Europa Clipper: launched October 14, 2024 on a Falcon Heavy, solar arrays 30.5 m tip to tip, gravity boosts from Mars (March 2025) and Earth (December 2026), arrival at Jupiter in April 2030, and 49 flybys of Europa as close as 25 km.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 96: Next stop, Olympus Mons. A volcano almost three times taller than Everest.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

Images: NASA (public domain)
Narration: AI voice

#space #europaclipper #astronomy #shorts #science

segments.text: NASA's biggest planetary spacecraft is racing to a moon that might have life.
On October fourteenth, twenty twenty-four, a Falcon Heavy rocket launched NASA's biggest planetary spacecraft ever.
segments.headline: Launch day

segments.text: With its solar panels open, Europa Clipper is thirty point five meters wide. Wider than a basketball court.
Its target is Europa, a moon of Jupiter with a salty ocean hidden under its ice.
segments.headline: The target: Europa

segments.text: Jupiter is so far away that Clipper needs help. In March twenty twenty-five, it swung past Mars to steal some speed.
segments.headline: A boost from Mars

segments.text: Then in December twenty twenty-six, it flew back past Earth for one last slingshot toward Jupiter.
segments.headline: A boost from Earth

segments.text: It arrives at Jupiter in April twenty thirty, after a journey of nearly three billion kilometers.
Then it will fly past Europa forty-nine times, as low as twenty-five kilometers above the ice.
It carries a vault to shield its electronics from Jupiter's radiation, and a poem engraved for the ocean world.
segments.headline: Shielded from radiation

segments.text: Tomorrow, we go back to Mars, to a volcano so big that if you stood on top, its base would disappear over the horizon. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
